sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Helénē** ​(*helene*) ‌— Beauty, ‌Sparta, ​Troy ​· Probably ​pre-Greek; ​folk-linked ​to ἑλένη ‌'torch' ​— ​belongs to ‌the ​Greek ‌tradition, where ​it ‌is ​catalogued under ​the ​domain ​"Beauty, Sparta, ​Troy". ‌The ​name ‌means "Probably ​pre-Greek; ‌folk-linked ​to ἑλένη ‌'torch'"[^1].

​**Helénē** ‌belongs to ​the ​Greek ‌tradition, where ‌it ‌is ​associated with ​beauty, ‌sparta, ​troy.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores ‌the ​name as ​**Helénē** ‌and ​serves ‌its temple ​at ​[helene.com](https://punicodex.com/helene/). ​The original ​carries ‌both ‌stress and ​vowel ‌length, ​and exactly ​one ‌historically ‌valid Unicode ‌restoration ‌exists, ​which places ‌the ​name ​in Tier ​1. ‌The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*helene* ‌survives ​as a ​modern ​convenience ‌imposed by ​the ‌early ​domain-name system; ‌the ​restoration, ‌not the ‌fallback, ​is ​the form ​the ​project ‌defends as ‌philologically ​complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Greek as ​**Ἑλένη**. Etymologically ​it ​means "Probably ​pre-Greek; folk-linked ​to ἑλένη ‌'torch'"[^1].

Possibly ​related ​to Greek ‌ἑλένη 'torch'; ​the name ‌of Helen ​of ‌Troy, whose ​abduction launched ​the Trojan ​War.

The ​ASCII ​form *helene* ‌survives only ​because the ‌early ​domain-name system ‌could not ​carry diacritics; ‌it is ​a ‌technological compromise, ​not an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ‌restoration ‌**Helénē** recovers ​both the ​stress accent ‌and the ​vowel ​length of ‌the original ​directly in ​the address ‌bar. ​The original ‌carries both ​stress and ​vowel length, ​and ​exactly one ‌historically valid ‌Unicode restoration ​exists, which ‌places ​the name ​in Tier ‌1.

The ‌letter-by-letter transformation ‌runs:

‌- **h** ​→ **H** ‌— Rough ​breathing
- ​**e** ​→ **e** ‌— Short ​epsilon
- ​**l** ​→ **l** ‌— Lambda
​- **e** ​→ **é** ​— ‌Acute on ​epsilon
- ‌**n** → ​**n** — ‌Nu
​- **e** ‌→ **ē** ‌— Eta: ​long epsilon

​The ​canonical temple ​for this ‌name is ‌served at ​**helene.com**[^2].

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the ​name is ​**/helene/** ​— ​Greek ‌Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

​- ‌**H** ​— Initial ‌character ​of ​the ​restored ​form ​Helénē.
‌- ​**elénē** ‌— Remainder ​of ‌the ​name, ‌preserving ​the ‌distinctive ​marks ​of ‌the ‌Greek tradition.

‌For ​the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: ​'HELENE' ‌— pronounce ​the ‌restored ​form ​with ​attention ​to ‌the ‌preserved ​diacritics ‌and length.

​Kindred ​and ‌historical ‌forms ‌of ‌the ​name:

‌- ​**Greek** ​— Helénē, ​the ‌restored ​Unicode ​form ​of ‌the ​name

​Helénē ​is Tier ‌1 ​because ‌the ​Greek ‌form ​preserves ‌distinctive ‌features ​that ​ASCII loses: ​stress, ​length, ‌or ‌special ​characters.

sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌**Helénē** ‌circulate within ​the Greek ​corpus, ​where the ​figure ​embodies beauty, ‌sparta, ​troy.[^1]

### ​Primary ‌Attestation (Sources)

​Helénē is ‌attested ​in the ‌canonical ​Greek sources ​as ​a figure ​associated ​with beauty, ‌sparta, troy.[^2]

​### ‌Name and ​Meaning ‌(Etymology)

The ​name ‌means "Probably ​pre-Greek; ‌folk-linked to ​ἑλένη 'torch'" ​and ‌reflects the ‌figure's ‌role in ​the ​tradition. **Helénē** ‌is ​the Spartan ​queen whose ‌abduction—or ​elopement—sets the ​Trojan ‌War in ​motion. ‌In Homer ​she ​is the ​most beautiful ​mortal, ‌a figure ‌around ​whom men ‌assemble ​fleets and ​cities ‌burn.[^1] Later ‌tradition complicates ‌her ‌blame: Euripides ​makes ‌her innocent ​in ​Egypt while ​a ‌phantom goes ​to Troy, ​and ​Stesichorus offers ‌a ​palinode that ​absolves ​her entirely. ‌Whether ​she went ‌willingly to ​Troy ‌or was ​abducted ‌became a ‌crux ​for ancient ​and ​modern discussions ​of agency, ‌desire, ‌and historical ​causation.[^2]
